title: IRS chief hasn't escaped impeachment yet
text:
The fate of embattled IRS Commissioner John Koskinen is likely to remain up in the air until at least November, as the divided Republican Party continues to debate what to do next following his impeachment hearing last week.
But after the election, Republican leaders could be forced once again by conservative lawmakers to consider the idea of impeaching Koskinen on the House floor.
A faction of House conservatives believes the hearing proved their argument that lawmakers should vote to impeach Koskinen because he oversaw the destruction of emails that Republicans were seeking related to the IRS targeting scandal.
"All we're asking is this guy no longer hold this office," Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, who is chairman of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, said after questioning Koskinen, who was under oath at the Wednesday hearing. "That's all we're asking. And in light of this fact pattern, I think that's the least we can do."
Jordan and others accuse Koskinen of lying under oath about efforts to preserve the emails, though Koskinen told the Judiciary Committee he wasn't aware those emails were destroyed when he made that pledge. "The statement was not correct in light of that evidence, which I did not know," Koskinen said at the hearing.
Still, Jordan told the Washington Examiner last week that he hasn't changed his mind about wanting to oust Koskinen. "We are committed to having a vote on impeachment," he said.
But the timing is uncertain, and it's not clear it will come to a vote. Conservatives cut a deal with GOP leadership to hold off a floor vote on impeachment in September in exchange for the Judiciary hearing.
Now that the hearing is over, House Judiciary Committee Chairman Bob Goodlatte, R-Va., will have to decide whether or when to schedule an impeachment vote at the committee level, which is the next step in an impeachment proceeding.
The House Republican conference is divided on the issue. Many GOP lawmakers still want to avoid an impeachment vote because they believe Koskinen's actions to not reach the threshold for such a rare punishment of an administration official.
A spokeswoman declined to comment last week on whether Goodlatte plans to schedule a committee vote.
Jordan said his immediate goal is to convince Goodlatte to let the Judiciary Committee hold a vote. "We know if we had the vote, we'd win," Jordan told the Examiner.
The articles of impeachment will be sent to the House floor if adopted by a majority vote of the Judiciary Committee.
Jordan said if the committee declines to hold the vote, Freedom Caucus members will bring it to the floor themselves, perhaps as soon as Congress returns for the lame-duck session after the November election. He played down the threat of Rep. Tim Huelskamp, R-Kansas, forcing an impeachment vote in the coming week, which he had pledged to do earlier this month.
Huelskamp told the Examiner last week he had not decided whether to bring up an impeachment vote in September, which he could do under a special floor procedure. It would require lawmakers to either table the vote, refer it back to the Judiciary Committee or vote on impeachment.
Jordan told the Examiner he "strongly discouraged" Huelskamp from bringing up the vote next week, which will likely be the last time the House is in session before the November election.
Huelskamp was the original co-sponsor of the resolution to vote on impeaching Koskinen along with Rep. John Fleming, R-La. Fleming said the hearing proved the Freedom Caucus case that Koskinen should go, but he stopped short of calling for impeachment.
"I think Congress and the American people received confirmation that their instincts were correct," Fleming said. "Koskinen should do the right thing and resign his office."
summary: The divided GOP continues to debate what to do next following John Koskinen's impeachment hearing last week.

title: Ivanovic parts with coach Kardon
text:
Ivanovic won the French Open last year after being runner-up in 2007
Ana Ivanovic has parted company with coach Craig Kardon after working with him for only four months.
Serbia's former world number one dropped out of the top 10 this week, following her fourth round exit from the French Open last month.
"I'd like to thank Craig for all his hard work, he's a great guy and I enjoyed working with him," said Ivanovic, now ranked 13th in the world.
Kardon is a former coach of Martina Navratilova and Lindsay Davenport.
Ivanovic, 21, last year won the French Open but has been unable to halt her slide down the world rankings.
606: DEBATE
Since last year's success at Roland Garros, she has since won just one event - the Linz Open last October.
The Serb has also been plagued by a persistent knee injury, resulting in her pulling out of the Madrid Open recently.
Her management company said she would be trained on a part-time basis by her sponsor's elite coaching staff during the grass court season including the Wimbledon championships which begin on 22 June.
The set-up includes Sven Groeneveld, who helped her during the 2008 season.

title: iPad 6 vs. iPad Air design in mockup
text:
Even though the iPad Air 2 will not be released until later this year, October being the most likely month of release, it is no surprise that we have already started to see a few mockups doing the rounds. From what we have seen so far, the changes to the 2014 full-size iPad will be subtle, although just enough to warrant some iOS users upgrading to the newer version.
Even though the new version will technically be an iPad 6 because it being the 6th generation model, it is more than likely to be known as the iPad Air 2 and we have come across a video that looks at the new mockup.
iPad Air 6 (Air 2) vs. original iPad Air — The video that we have embedded for you below looks at the new dummy unit of the upcoming iPad Air 2 and puts it up against the current Air to see just how different they are in terms of design.
We have already seen a few images of this last week, but it is far better to see it for yourself with a video, as it seems to make it more real, even though it is not.
Size wise, they are both the same, although the iPad Air 2, or iPad 6 as some people will call it seems to be thinner than the current model, although this might not end up being the case seeing as though dummy models tend to be slightly thinner because they have no hardware inside.
There are some subtle changes between the two though, such as the Touch ID button and differences to the volume buttons to the side, as well as the rotation lock switch now being missing. We know that many of you use this all the time and by doing away with it could lose Apple customers, but what’s wrong with using rotation lock in the control center?

title: New Nintendo NX Console More Powerful Than PS4? Latest Leaks & More
text:
The Nintendo NX has been a subject of many rumors recently. Apparently, many people are excited to see the console in the flesh. There are some leaks online but not so much on how it looks. The leaks claim that the said machine is more powerful than its Sony counterpart, the PS4. This was posted in
The detail was posted in a NX reddit forum. The thread has been swarmed with other Redditors and there might have been some wrong information in the poster’s original comments that could prove it wrong. The original poster may have been wrong or doesn’t know the specs too well.
The rumors have been circulating these past few months and new updates continue to surface that Nintendo has lessened Wii U production this year. Wii U has really lost its touch as its sales continue to plummet down. The Wii U offered almost the same power as the Xbox 360 and PS3 but there is no reason that the Nintendo NX can’t compete with the power of the Xbox One and PS4. Nintendo has been known to build small, simple systems with great hardware performing almost the same as its rivals.
This means that the Wii U has roughly the same performance as the previous generations consoles with some small differences. The small design differences have decided the winners and its only main advantage is the motion controllers which made it unique (the Xbox One and PS4 has caught up with that advantage and sells motion sensors now too). The Nintendo NX has been a great local multiplayer past time, though.
The Nintendo NX has now emphasized on its power to catch up with its competition. The company wanted to create a console will help it stand out from the rest, but we hope to see them compatible with HDTVs with higher resolution and great detail as soon as it launches in the market.
summary: The Nintendo NX has been rumored to be more powerful Sony's PS4. A reddit post has claimed that the console is "slightly" more powerful than its rival.

title: 'Can't deal with food adulteration'
text:
Say officials from Noida authority, even as usage of sub-standard items rises in festive season
Say officials from Noida authority, even as usage of sub-standard items rises in festive season
Avoid sweetmeats and other milk products this festive season. It's not just about watching your weight. With Diwali a few days away, food adulteration has become rampant. Items such as khoya, mawa, paneer etc are the first casualties. Authorities in Noida acknowledge this fact. But officials allege nothing can be done as they are not equipped to handle the problem.
Officials from the food and civil supplies department say that most of these products are manufactured in far-flung and remote areas located 60-70 km from the Noida main city. "For conducting raids to stop adulteration, we need to go to such places. But we don't have government vehicles for that," said an official, on condition of anonymity.
Rough ride
"We were even assured that a vehicle would be given to us but we are still waiting for. The moment it comes to us, raids will be conducted and all the traders involved in such acts will be booked," he added. Though Noida food inspector AK Jaiswal avoided commenting on the issue, he cautioned consumers from buying adulterated products. "People should see to it that they don't fall into the trap of shopkeepers selling cheap products. They should rather buy from renowned places and check the quality thoroughly," he advised.
When the festive and marriage season merge, demand of sweet items and other milk products rises exponentially. From 30-40 tonnes in the summer months, it jumps to over 70 tonnes in this season. In a surprise check conducted five months ago by Noida's food and civil supplies department, it was found that more than 50 per cent of the samples collected from reputed shops failed the laboratory test. In all 75 food samples were sent for testing and the result showed that at least half of them were adulterated and sub-standard. Twelve FIRs were lodged and legal action was initiated.
What to do?
Meanwhile, consumers are aware, but say they have few choices. Romesh Kumar, a sector-62 resident said, "Cases of adulteration are more these days as the supply of milk products is less than half of the demand. But we are left with no option but to buy them as it is an important item in the kitchen during festive season."
Others suggested that consumer awareness drives should be organised at this time of the year to educate citizens on how to differentiate between good quality and adulterated food products. Several factories and offices have also stopped buying sweets for their employees during festivals. Organisations now prefer to give away dry fruits or other gift items.
Watch what you eat
Adulteration of food means cheating the consumer and poses a serious health risk. It is a punishable offence under the provisions of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Such cases are decided within three months and the official can fine the culprit with a maximum of Rs 3 lakh and in case of adulteration, which is injurious to health the fine can be of a maximum of Rs 10 lakh.
summary: Say officials from Noida authority, even as usage of sub-standard items rises in festive season

title: Absence of ministers again annoys Senate chairman
text:
ISLAMABAD: Days after the prime minister’s directions to his cabinet members to accord priority to parliamentary business after Senate Chairman Raza Rabbani threatened to resign in protest against what he called efforts to demean the upper house of parliament, absence of ministers and lack of responses to questions put by Senators prompted the chairman to say on Wednesday that he was ready if the government wanted to repeat Friday’s episode.
During the question hour, Mr Rabbani became angry to see that no response to a question already deferred thrice earlier had been given. Through his question Farhatullah Babar had sought to know the details of pension and other benefits admissible to officers of the rank of major general and above of the Pakistan Army, Navy and Air Force on their retirement.
A brief and written answer from Defence Minister Khawaja Asif, who was not present in the house, merely said the information was being collected and would be provided as soon as it was received.
The information had been sought after reports suggested that former army chief retired General Raheel Sharif had been allotted 90 acres of agriculture land along Bedian road in Lahore and the ISPR’s clarification that there was nothing unusual in the allotment.
“What is the information being collected? This is a question pertaining to a general policy and they do not have an answer to that,” Mr Rabbani remarked. He addressed Parliamentary Affairs Minister Sheikh Aftab Ahmad, who was responding on behalf of the defence minister, and said that if the government wanted a repeat of Friday’s episode he was ready for it.
Minister of State for Interior Baleeghur Rehman said: “We do not want it” and observed that things were improving. Mr Rabbani, however, pointed out that responses to several questions pertaining to his ministry, including the one about perks and privileges of the Nadra chairman, had also not been received.
Another question which did not receive a reply was “whether it is a fact that the employees and pensioners of the Heavy Mechanical Complex, Taxila, are not being paid their salaries and pensions; if so, the reasons thereof indicating also the number of affected employees and pensioners and the time since which they have not been paid their salaries and pensions; and (b) the steps being taken by the government to pay salaries and pensions to the said employees?”. The question had been asked by Chaudhry Tanvir Khan of PML-N.
“Is this classified information? What should I do? Why should I not suspend the question hour?” an angry Mr Rabbani asked. He directed chairman of the senate’s standing committee on rules, procedures and privileges Jehanzaib Jamaldini to summon the defence secretary and ask him why replies were not being submitted.
Soon after this, Azam Swati’s question about the number of persons deputed for tree plantation, looking after flower beds or other related work in Islamabad was responded to and the house was informed that 972 gardeners were working in the horticulture branch of the Metropolitan Corporation, Islamabad.
The Senate chairman addressed Mr Swati and said: “You are lucky that your question has been answered.” Members of the house thumped their desks at this. Mr Rabbani, however, said the reply had been received as it pertained to information about gardeners.
Absence of the Kashmir affairs minister also annoyed the chairman who said they did not read the prime minister’s letter carefully, which talked of giving priority to parliamentary business. He was also irked by the absence of the members whose questions had to be deferred because they were absent. He said he was evolving a procedure under which the absence of members with their questions on agenda would face penalty.
He said question hour was the most important part of the parliamentary proceedings.
Published in Dawn, April 20th, 2017
summary: Rabbani became angry to see that no response to a question already deferred thrice earlier had been given.

title: Stéphane Sessègnon drives the final nail into Paolo Di Canio's coffin
text:
This was the defeat that proved too much for Sunderland's owner to bear. Even if the performance was not quite as bad as the scoreline suggests, the display featured many of the shortcomings that undermined Paolo Di Canio's short tenure as manager: lack of fluency, quality, luck and harmony. It did not help Di Canio's cause that Albion, who came into the game as the only other winless team in the Premier League, highlighted the qualities that Sunderland were missing.
The visitors actually started the game well, their players' dynamism seemingly justifying Di Canio's intensive fitness training and giving no hint of dressing room discontent with his confrontational man management. But they could not find enough creativity to turn possession into penetration and, in contrast, Albion scored from their first real attack, the ball being swept into the net by the debutant Stéphane Sessègnon, who was sold by Di Canio a month ago because of his perceived "bad attitude".
There was no lack of effort from the Benin international here, partially, perhaps, because Di Canio had been unable to restrain himself from criticising Sessègnon in public during the build-up. If that helped motivate an opponent, most of Di Canio's public outbursts seemed to sap his own team's morale, as continually being ridiculed for their mistakes resulted in brittle confidence. There were signs of that here too as, after falling behind, Sunderland shrivelled up.
Di Canio attributed the team's coyness to two factors: their unfamiliarity with each other – which is understandable in a club that signed 14 new players in the summer – and the players' reluctance to communicate with each other, an affliction that Di Canio – showcasing his own unique idea of effective communication – reckoned would be resolved once they "clear the rubbish from their brains".
Sunderland did eventually mount a rally of sorts but Steven Fletcher fired over from close range and dislocated his shoulder as he fell. Just as a wrongly disallowed goal turned Sunderland's previous match in favour of Arsenal, the unfortunate loss of Fletcher gave Albion added impetus, with Sunderland forced to play on with 10 men.
Liam Ridgewell doubled the hosts' lead two minutes later after excellent work by Morgan Amalfitano, who crowned the victory by plundering the third goal himself. The performance of Amalfitano and Albion's other recruits – Sessègnon, Scott Sinclair and Victor Anichebe – emphasised the travails of Sunderland's newcomers, who have not yet struck up such cohesion, nor showed signs of similar quality. Perhaps Di Canio bought too many new players at the same time? Or perhaps he bought badly? Still, Di Canio's employers sanctioned his radical overhaul of the squad, presumably because they believed a revolution was necessary. Many of Sunderland's fans agreed, which is why only a few of those at The Hawthorns called for Di Canio's head to roll.
In fact, the manager, who walked over to them at the end of the game to tell them "pick me, blame me, leave the players", was surprised by the restraint of the majority. "I did much worse when I was a fan," he said. "I can't tell you what I did, otherwise they are going to arrest me."
Yet Di Canio saw no reason for him to quit. He believed results would improve once the players fully absorbed his plans and personality. "I always believe I am the best manager in the world," he said. "Why should I have to walk out? I have been working 24 hours a day. The 24 players have to adapt to me. The players have to adapt to one person. Which regime works in a way where the 24 players decide, 'We want to play in our way'?" Sunderland apparently decided Di Canio was no longer the man to inspire such unity. Given that he was in charge for only 13 matches the club can hardly be said to have shown much patience. But, then, that was never Di Canio's style either.
Man of the match Morgan Amalfitano (West Bromwich Albion)
summary: Sunderland's 3-0 defeat at West Bromwich Albion proved to be Paolo Di Canio's final match in charge

title: Rez Infinite is out now on PC, as we interview creator Tetsuya Mizuguchi
text:
Rez Infinite – finally available on PC
GameCentral interviews the creator of Lumines about the new PC version of Rez, and how he was influenced by New Order and Xenon 2.
One of the downsides of writing about video games for a living is that you rarely get a chance to go back and play your favourites. But we always like to make an exception for Rez. The mix of rhythm action and on-rails shooter was first released on the Dreamcast in 2001, and we’ve always tried to go back and play through it again at least once every year. Something that’s been made easier by just how many times it’s been re-released in the last 15 years. And yet this is the first time it’s ever been on PC…
Rez Infinite is available on Steam right now, and although in terms of content it’s the same game that was released on PlayStation 4 last year this version runs at 4K and 60 frames per second, has double the texture resolution, and is compatible with both Oculus Rift and HTC Rift. The latter is important because although the game is playable without VR the all-new Area X stage is one of the best virtual reality experiences we’ve ever had.
You can read our full review of the PlayStation 4 version here, but we also recently had a chance to talk to Rez creator Tetsuya Mizuguchi about his unusual career in games and his obsession with synaesthesia – experiencing stimuli with different senses than the norm, such as seeing sounds as colours or colours as smells.
Naturally, we also asked him about what he’s working on next, and his experiences developing for the PC and virtual reality. Not to mention his other plans for Rez and the future of interactive entertainment.
Formats: PlayStation 4 and PC
Price: £19.99
Publisher: Enhance Games
Developer: Monstars Inc. and Resonair
Release Date: 9th August 2017
Age Rating: 7
(Mizuguchi-san speaks English well enough to not need an interpreter, but seems surprisingly nervous when asking us what we thought of Rez Infinite on PlayStation 4.)
GC: Yeah, it was all right.
TM: …
GC: By which I mean it’s probably the best VR experience I’ve ever had. [laughs]
TM: [laughs]
GC: Rez is honestly one of my favourite games ever. But let’s begin with how you started in the games industry. I get the impression your primary interest is music rather than gameplay, so how did you end up at Sega making driving games? Did you take that job hoping you would get the chance to make something more personal later?
TM: I am a music lover, and when I was young I wanted to be a music video director. I got a big, big influence from the first generation of MTV. There I saw a new kind of expression, that combined sound and music and visual storytelling. I was especially influenced by artists from the UK, like New Order and their amazing videos. I was in Japan but they were a big influence, as they already were able to show a new form of artistic expression. So I wanted to create something like that too, not a music video but something that would only be possible using future technology.
So I decided to get into the game industry, and for the first 10 years I produced racing games like Sega Rally. These were arcade games using new 3D technology that was very advanced for the time. But I couldn’t give up on creating something new, my concept of combining music and visuals. So then I decided to move on from racing games and I had two inspirations I wanted to make: a musical, which was Space Channel 5, and a game where the music is a very deep element of the gameplay, which became Rez.
If you’re a musician playing instruments with somebody, and making a groove, it feels good and I wanted to recreate that in a game. So I needed to break that feeling down into smaller elements and processes. Not just musicians, but also a DJ playing music and people dancing to it. So, we factorised many things. I combined as much as I could into Rez and playing the game: playing the instruments, getting into the groove, experiencing the music, the changing back track, and the shooting and visual changes. And all of this was to create a kind of synaesthesia.
The synaesthesia concept started from Rez. So then I made Lumines on PSP and Child Of Eden with Kinect technology, and now we have VR and high res 4K. So the experience is getting better and better with each new technology. I think now the situation is the best it has ever been in my life. [laughs] And I already have 27 years in this industry.
Advertisement
But back to the original question… I love music very much. But I wanted to make a new experience and I thought games would be the best place to start to create that. Games combined not only with sounds and visuals but also vibration and haptic technology. And then if we have the new technology, maybe 8K in the future [laughs] or AR, MR… it’s getting better and better all the time, and that means we can create an illusion that is better and better also.
GC: You mention some of your musical influences, but what about specific video game influences? The basic gameplay of Rez is quite similar to Panzer Dragoon and other Sega shooters, so where you using inspiration from games like that to create a foundation for your new concept?
TM: I’m not a heavy gamer, but I always loved games in terms of the culture and new technology. I played one game when I was a student in… ’87, maybe. That game was Xenon 2.
GC: Xenon 2?! By The Bitmap Brothers?
TM: Yeah! [laughs] And Bomb the Bass. I was so shocked to see these artists already creating a new kind of expression, using music with games.
GC: It seems British artists had a lot of influence on your career.
TM: Yes! [laughs]
GC: But the thing about Xenon 2 is it wasn’t a particularly good game, but the music, and the fact that it was licensed music, made it very memorable.
TM: That’s true. But, in my imagination, I thought about how if you played the game well you could change the music and make it even better. But what kind of game would that be? That was the first inspiration for Rez. I also enjoyed Xevious from Namco, so I had the idea of a shooting game that worked with music, but that was all.
Advertisement
And maybe 15 years later I went to Zürich, and I encountered a huge rave music party called the Street Parade. There was techno music there, and I was not a techno music fan at the time but it did make an impression on me. Over 100,000 people were dancing in the town, and at night everybody moved to a huge stadium. Everyone was dancing but there was also the changing sounds and the changing colours, and I got the inspiration that this is like a Kandinsky painting. Not only him, but the other Bauhaus artists.
100 years ago many artists talked about synaesthesia and the cross multi-modal feeling, and Kandinsky’s paintings were often inspired by sound. So I think we had the same inspiration and expression. But 100 years ago Kandinsky just had one canvas to work on, but now technology gives us much more. So I thought: what kind of experience can I make that will be the next step? And then I remembered Xenon 2 and Xevious. And that was 1997.
And then I started to think, ‘What kind of game should I make?’ And then I tried a few prototypes but I decided, ‘OK, let’s make a shooter, but this is like a new shooter’. It should be like playing instruments, shooting sound effects, getting the music automatically, and with visuals that react. And then you get the vibration from the controller as well. So the inspiration was growing and growing like that.
GC: What were some of the earlier prototypes like? Did you ever consider making Rez a 2D shooter?
TM: No, it was always 3D. That was the PlayStation 2 and Dreamcast era, where 3D was still quite new. The music we had at first was not gorgeous, so I decided to use techno sounds. And it was obvious that was a good match.
GC: Video games tend to age very quickly, so it’s fascinating to me that Rez seems so ageless. Especially as it has what was at the time a contemporary soundtrack. How is it that the game has never seemed to date?
TM: I wanted to make a timeless game, and a timeless game means not trying to chase current trends. We needed good music but also maybe a sound that was a little abstract. So I travelled around and met some people in the UK. I met Adam Freeland in Brighton and I met Coldcut here in London, and also some musicians from Japan and Germany. I had a conversion with Coldcut and Adam Freeland, and found they are not typical musicians.
Colduct had been thinking about synesthesia too, and how to make a unique expression. How can we expand and combine music with visuals? And what can you feel when you do that? Those were important conversations, so we got a big, big inspiration from them. We were inspired by them, we wanted to create that kind of world and experience using their music. But when we got the music from them we cut it up and edited it to use in the game, which seemed wrong at first, so that players could finalise the music by playing.
GC: Rez is over 15 years old now, and was released the same year as Harmonix’s Frequency, which means it’s now outlasted the entire music game genre. Why do you think rhythm action games turned out to be just a fad?
TM: I think they needed some fresh ideas, in order to go to the next level. The first generation of music-based games used icons on the screen, but I never liked that. This is not synesthesia. But today visuals are so realistic and detailed that just watching icons move over the top of them seems less interesting. So that style of game needed to evolve, to become more integrated.
GC: You went straight from Space Channel 5, which did have icons of a sort, to Rez, but you’re right, the rest of the industry never even made that first step.
TM: Yeah.
GC: It’s clear your interest is in trying to excite all the sense at once, but that’s always included a sexual element as well. I don’t know how you ever convinced Sega to sell the trance vibrator.
TM: [laughs]
GC: And I seem to remember at an event for Child Of Eden you had a bunch of Xbox 360 controllers stuffed down your trousers.
TM: [laughs] That’s right, while playing with Kinect. We have also made synesthesia suits and they have 26 vibrators built into them.
GC: …
TM: [laughs] You can feel the sound texture, like bass, and drum, and guitar – any type of sounds you can feel. So if you play Rez wearing the suit you get the first beat just under here [points to body] and then you shoot the cube and you get the music and the high hat around the shoulder. So the sound texture is moving with the music. So sometimes your body is like a guitar. I think that everybody that played Rez Infinite should experience it this way. This is one of my dreams, to give everyone this totally new synesthesia experience. It’s something we almost have no words to describe yet, but it will be a future experience.
The trance vibrator – gaming’s most infamous controller
GC: How close is using the suit to your perfect Rez experience? Or are you still waiting for new technology to become available?
TM: Still waiting, it’s not enough! [laughs] I think VR is a big, big revolution. Because we’ve had almost 130 years of cinematic media, and until now it has not evolved. So that was always a big frustration to me. When I made Child Of Eden I tried 3D on PS3, but that was like just watching something through a window – which was not fun. But now we can create everything as if you are in the world with it, although the resolution is not enough yet. But this is just the beginning.
GC: Is there anything else specifically you’re waiting for or do you just look at new technology and then think how you can use that with Rez?
TM: Hmm… that’s a very interesting question. I like to use the improvements from new technology all the time. But now I’m waiting for new technology after basic VR, mainly the resolution. We need to get from HD to 4K and from 4K to 8K. And when we have 8K for each eye, I think that is enough. I think that is kind of the singularity point. If we get to 8K it looks real and we can make a true illusion.
But I want to create more, if you can move and feel in 3D space maybe you can touch the sounds, you can touch the music. So in the future we can create a new type of experience. Whether that is a game or a new type of entertainment though, I don’t know.
GC: So, Area X. How did you go about designing that? Was that an idea you had already that you were finally able to visualise or did you just create it from scratch?
TM: This was from scratch. But I decided a few things first: let’s generate a bunch of particles so we can see the music and sound. That kind of experience is now possible. So we generate many, many particles and they all react to the sound of the music. So that’s number one and number two is, ‘Okay, let’s make the game so you can move freely’.
So the original Rez was a rail shooter, but Area X is free. It’s like swimming, like flying like Peter Pan. In a rail shooter it’s easy to make the music work with the gameplay, but if you can move freely how can we make an experience with the music building? That was a big challenge.
GC: The other thing that impressed me is that there’s no nausea problems at all, despite the fact you’re moving in 3D. How did you manage that?
TM: Maybe we have luck. [laughs] We experimented a little bit first, and tried to discover why we feel sick. But we had some assumptions too, that making a game like a FPS will inevitably make you feel sick. I think that our brain can’t calibrate properly when it’s being told it’s walking or interacting with normal floors and walls that aren’t there. So in a way something impossible like Rez’s movement is less of an issue. I think one of the reasons we feel sick is we’re fighting with our brain’s prejudice! [laughs]
GC: You seem to be implying you worked all this out intuitively. Normally when I speak to VR developers they’ve read through all kinds of medical documents, and they’re very clinical about it all. Your approach seems much more rock ‘n’ roll.
TM: [laughs] Maybe we do have luck.
GC: [laughs] Well, that seems a much more artistic approach.
TM: So in my head the new Rez experience must have a flying or swimming element, and if VR cannot do that then maybe it’s not the future media after all.
GC: You must be happy it did work out then!
TM: [laughs]
GC: So Rez Infinite is out on PC now, but what else are you working on at the moment? I understand you teach at a university now?
TM: I have just a regular tenure for doing projects, which has included the synesthesia suits. So I have worked with the students to design those and other haptic devices.
GC: Would you still describe yourself as a game developer?
TM: I love to make games.
GC: I love to play them, so I’d like you to make some more.
TM: [laughs] But after Child Of Eden I wanted a fresh breath. I needed a change. So I stopped any creation and started to teach at the university, not only games but also media design. Any type of new tech and the future. And the students gave me a fresh inspiration and that was really good. And then – maybe three years I taught at university – and then I started a new studio called Enhance Games, which is focusing on VR and new experiences.
GC: So we may see brand new games in the future?
TM: Sure, yes.
GC: Do you think we’ll ever see anything that could be called Rez 2?
TM: Not yet. [laughs] But I have a list… We are already doing a new project now, and preparing other future projects beyond that. This is a very exciting time for me, I think the best ever. Especially as I get to keep my creations.
GC: Will this be primarily for the PC or consoles?
TM: All platforms. This is the first time we’ve made a PC version. Many gamers exist in the world, so we can really expand the experience into other audiences. So I’m a little bit nervous, because I’m used to console gamers but this is the first time with PC gamers. But I think this is also the future: the PC, including VR technology. So I want to keep our console relationship but also explore into the PC area.
GC: You mentioned retaining the rights to your games in the future, but do you have the rights to Child Of Eden?
TM: No, Ubisoft have the IP.
GC: So you couldn’t make a Child Of Eden Infinite without them?
TM: [laughs] You want that?
GC: Yeah, I do! I really liked it. Are you implying you weren’t happy with it?
TM: No, no. I’m very happy with it. Child Of Eden is like a spiritual sequel, so that means that if we make the new next future, next Rez, it would maybe be a sequel to both Rez and Child Of Eden. I think so.
GC: Well, please don’t take 15 years to make it.
TM: [laughs] OK, I promise!
GC: Thanks very much for you time, it’s been great to meet you.
TM: Thank you.
Email gamecentral@ukmetro.co.uk, leave a comment below, and follow us on Twitter
summary: GameCentral interviews the creator of Lumines about the new PC version of Rez, and how he was influenced by New Order and Xenon 2.

title: Hollywood Reacts to GOP Debate as Jokes, Takedowns and Questions Flood Twitter
text:
Millions of eyes across the nation were on the GOP debate on Wednesday, and that included both supporters and critics in Hollywood.
As the media analyzed every word uttered by lead candidates Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Paul Rand, Carly Fiorina and Jeb Bush, stars voiced their opinions on social media.
Also Read: 6 Things Scene and Heard at CNN's GOP Debate
Tom Hanks, Emma Watson and Patton Oswalt watched CNN’s coverage of the debate from the set of “The Circle,” wearing concerned and “confused” expressions as they posted a selfie.
Minnie Driver hoped that someone would put Air Force One, which the candidates stood in front of throughout the debate, to good use. “Does that plane work? Can it take them all away at the end to place where everyone is white and there are no women,” she asked on Twitter.
Comedian Kathy Griffin made no secret about who her mother was voting for at least. “My mom would only vote for Donald Trump if she was extremely drunk. She is #ReadyForHillary,” she tweeted as the debate kicked off.
Meanwhile Maria Shriver, former First Lady of California, pointed out that there are several people “running for President who have never held any office before.”
Also Read: Jimmy Kimmel Compares the Packed GOP Debate to 'American Idol'
Like many Americans, “Real Housewives of Beverly Hills” star Lisa Rinna was driven to drink by the debate, and Jesse Ventura suggested the candidates chill out and smoke some weed.
The debate also sparked hilarious hashtags such as #MakeASongGOP, which suggested “Shine on You Crazy Donald” and “End of the World as We Know it,” as Trump’s theme song.
Scott Walker referred to reality show “The Apprentice” when he slammed real estate mogul Trump by saying: “we don’t need an ‘Apprentice’ in the White House we have one right now,” and the phrase quickly sparked a Twitter trend reiterating his opinion.
